variants.title: Complete the lifecycle
variants.context: MCP is stateful, so initialization comes first: the client proposes a version, the server answers with a version and its capabilities, the client sends notifications/initialized, and only then do normal requests begin. Each side may use only what was negotiated for that session.
variants.prompt: A host opens a new connection to a document server. Put the lifecycle steps in order.

items.text: The server answers with a version it supports, its implementation information, and its server capabilities.
The client sends initialize with its latest supported protocol version, client information, and client capabilities.
Both sides operate inside the negotiated version and capabilities, applying local policy and request timeouts.
The client sends notifications/initialized to mark the session ready for normal traffic.

variants.hint: One message separates negotiation from normal operation.
variants.explanation: Initialization has a fixed order, and tools, resources, and prompts requests should not begin before the session is acknowledged.

variants.title: Complete the lifecycle
variants.context: MCP is stateful, so initialization comes first: the client proposes a version, the server answers with a version and its capabilities, the client sends notifications/initialized, and only then do normal requests begin. Each side may use only what was negotiated for that session.
variants.prompt: A Streamable HTTP server returns 404 for a request that carries a known MCP-Session-Id. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: Send notifications/initialized, then resume tools, resources, and prompts requests under the new session.
Read the 404 as an expired session rather than as a transport hiccup worth retrying with the same ID.
Discard the stored session ID and any client state that depended on that session.
Send a fresh initialize request without the expired ID and read the version and capabilities that come back.

variants.hint: One message separates negotiation from normal operation.
variants.explanation: An expired session is restarted through the full lifecycle, because the negotiated state it depended on no longer exists.

variants.title: Complete the lifecycle
variants.context: MCP is stateful, so initialization comes first: the client proposes a version, the server answers with a version and its capabilities, the client sends notifications/initialized, and only then do normal requests begin. Each side may use only what was negotiated for that session.
variants.prompt: A host wants notifications when a server's tool list changes. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The server returns its capabilities, advertising tools together with the listChanged subfeature.
The client sends initialize and declares the capabilities it is prepared to support.
The client acknowledges with notifications/initialized before issuing any tools request.
The client expects tool list change notifications only because listChanged was advertised for this session.

variants.hint: One message separates negotiation from normal operation.
variants.explanation: Subfeatures are negotiated separately, so a related primitive is never enough reason to expect a notification.

variants.title: Cross the authorization boundary
variants.context: MCP authorization protects HTTP transport access, but a valid bearer token does not prove that this user intended this call. The host reviews intent, the token is audience-bound to the MCP server, server policy checks the operation, and any upstream API needs its own credential.
variants.prompt: A host calls a remote MCP server that updates a CRM record. Put the boundary crossings in order.

items.text: The server acquires a separate credential for the CRM API instead of forwarding the client's MCP token.
The user and host review the server, the requested scopes, the tool inputs, the target, and the side effect.
The request carries a token whose OAuth resource is the canonical MCP server URI, and the server validates that audience.
Server policy validates inputs, user and tenant scope, resource ownership, rate limits, and the current approval record.

variants.hint: Ask which credential each hop is actually allowed to present.
variants.explanation: Transport authorization and operation authorization are different checks, and token passthrough to a downstream API is forbidden.

variants.title: Cross the authorization boundary
variants.context: MCP authorization protects HTTP transport access, but a valid bearer token does not prove that this user intended this call. The host reviews intent, the token is audience-bound to the MCP server, server policy checks the operation, and any upstream API needs its own credential.
variants.prompt: A tool call returns insufficient_scope. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: Start a visible step-up authorization flow that includes the resource parameter and PKCE for a public client.
Stop replaying the same token, because looping it cannot add a scope the token never carried.
Validate the new token's issuer, audience, expiry, signature, and the scope this operation requires.
Retry the call under server-side policy checks and an approval that covers this specific effect.

variants.hint: Ask which credential each hop is actually allowed to present.
variants.explanation: An insufficient scope is a consent problem, so it is fixed by a visible step-up flow rather than by retrying the same token.

variants.title: Cross the authorization boundary
variants.context: MCP authorization protects HTTP transport access, but a valid bearer token does not prove that this user intended this call. The host reviews intent, the token is audience-bound to the MCP server, server policy checks the operation, and any upstream API needs its own credential.
variants.prompt: A user approves a file-writing tool for one project directory. Put the enforcement steps in order.

items.text: Every inbound request is authenticated and its token audience is verified against this MCP server.
The server validates the resource URI and tool inputs against the paths it is permitted to touch.
The host records approval that is specific to this client and these scopes, not reused from an unrelated grant.
The process sandbox enforces the same limits, because roots are coordination hints rather than a filesystem sandbox.

variants.hint: Ask which credential each hop is actually allowed to present.
variants.explanation: Path limits are enforced in the host, the sandbox, and the server, since a declared root only tells a server where to work.

variants.title: Own the primitive
variants.context: MCP server primitives differ by who initiates them: resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled, and tools are model-controlled. Clients can also offer features back to servers, such as elicitation, roots, and sampling.
variants.prompt: A host team is documenting its MCP integration. Match each feature to who initiates its use.

pairs.label: Resources
pairs.detail: The client lists or reads a URI and decides whether the result belongs in model context.

pairs.label: Prompts
pairs.detail: A user explicitly selects a reusable template, and the client fetches its arguments and messages.

pairs.label: Tools
pairs.detail: The model requests a schema-described function, and the host may show inputs, apply policy, or deny it.

pairs.label: Client features
pairs.detail: The server asks the host for elicitation, roots, or sampling, but only when that feature was negotiated.

variants.hint: Ask who starts the interaction, not who executes it.
variants.explanation: Ownership decides the consent model: application-controlled, user-controlled, and model-controlled features need different review.

variants.title: Own the primitive
variants.context: MCP server primitives differ by who initiates them: resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled, and tools are model-controlled. Clients can also offer features back to servers, such as elicitation, roots, and sampling.
variants.prompt: Match each primitive to the host behavior it requires in a consent design.

pairs.label: Resources
pairs.detail: Validate the URI and decide, application side, whether the fetched content enters the model's context.

pairs.label: Prompts
pairs.detail: Surface the template so the user chooses it deliberately, then resolve its declared arguments.

pairs.label: Tools
pairs.detail: Intercept the model's request, display the arguments and target, and obtain consent before execution.

pairs.label: Client features
pairs.detail: Negotiate each reverse request surface deliberately and keep user review inside the loop.

variants.hint: Ask who starts the interaction, not who executes it.
variants.explanation: The host decides which primitives reach the model and what still needs approval, no matter what the handshake allowed.

variants.title: Own the primitive
variants.context: MCP server primitives differ by who initiates them: resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled, and tools are model-controlled. Clients can also offer features back to servers, such as elicitation, roots, and sampling.
variants.prompt: Match each product need to the MCP feature that fits it.

pairs.label: Read a project schema file into context
pairs.detail: Resources, listed and read by the application before the model sees them.

pairs.label: Run a saved triage workflow the user picks from a menu
pairs.detail: Prompts, chosen by the user and expanded by the client.

pairs.label: Let the model file a ticket during a conversation
pairs.detail: Tools, requested by the model and gated by host policy and consent.

pairs.label: Let a server ask the user for a missing field
pairs.detail: Elicitation, a client feature that must be negotiated for the session.

variants.hint: Ask who starts the interaction, not who executes it.
variants.explanation: Choosing the primitive by its initiator keeps consent and presentation aligned with who actually asked for the action.

variants.title: Capability is not authority
variants.context: Capability is not authority. A successful handshake proves both sides understand a protocol feature. It does not prove the server is trustworthy, that a token has the right audience, or that a particular call is approved.
variants.prompt: An unvetted server advertises a tool annotated readOnlyHint. How should the host treat that annotation?
options: As untrusted metadata, with risk enforced from a host-owned tool inventory.
As grounds for lowering the approval requirement by one risk tier.
As proof the tool cannot change state, so consent can be skipped.
optionFeedback: Right: annotations are hints from the server itself, so an untrusted server cannot set its own risk class.
Partly trusting an unverifiable claim still lets the server choose its own risk class.
The server that would make the change is the same party making the claim.
variants.hint: Ask who authored the evidence you are about to rely on.
variants.explanation: Tool annotations are hints, not proof, so risk comes from a host-owned inventory unless the server itself is trusted.

variants.title: Capability is not authority
variants.context: Capability is not authority. A successful handshake proves both sides understand a protocol feature. It does not prove the server is trustworthy, that a token has the right audience, or that a particular call is approved.
variants.prompt: A Streamable HTTP server issues an MCP-Session-Id and later requests arrive carrying it. What does that identifier establish?
options: That the caller is the same authenticated subject that initialized the session.
That the caller may skip authentication until the session expires.
Protocol state only, so every request still needs its own authentication.
optionFeedback: A session ID can be replayed by anyone who obtains it, so it proves nothing about the subject.
Authorization is verified on every inbound HTTP request, not once per session.
Right: session IDs coordinate protocol state and must never be accepted as proof of identity.
variants.hint: Ask who authored the evidence you are about to rely on.
variants.explanation: Session IDs are rotated or expired random coordination values, and session state is bound to an authenticated subject.

variants.title: Capability is not authority
variants.context: Capability is not authority. A successful handshake proves both sides understand a protocol feature. It does not prove the server is trustworthy, that a token has the right audience, or that a particular call is approved.
variants.prompt: A host declares one directory as a root and concludes the server cannot read anything outside it. What is wrong?
options: Roots must be declared during initialize, so a later declaration never applies.
Roots are coordination hints, so paths must be enforced in the host, sandbox, and server.
Roots cover resources only, so the server's tools remain unconstrained by them.
optionFeedback: The timing of the declaration is not what makes a root non-binding.
Right: a root tells a server where to work, and by itself it is not an enforcement boundary.
The gap is enforcement, not which primitive a root happens to cover.
variants.hint: Ask who authored the evidence you are about to rely on.
variants.explanation: Roots are hints, so filesystem limits are enforced independently by the host, the process sandbox, and the server.

variants.title: Operate the transport
variants.context: The data layer stays JSON-RPC, but the transport changes connection ownership, authentication, and failure behavior. stdio launches a local subprocess; Streamable HTTP exposes one endpoint over POST and GET with optional server-sent events.
variants.prompt: A desktop application needs a server that reads local project files for one user, with no network exposure. Which transport fits?
options: Streamable HTTP on a public port, protected by a bearer token.
stdio, with a pinned executable, a constrained environment, and a sandbox.
Streamable HTTP with server-sent events so file changes can stream.
optionFeedback: Publishing a local-only capability on a public port adds an attack surface the task never needed.
Right: a local subprocess keeps the connection, the credentials, and the file access on the user's machine.
Streaming is a message pattern, not a reason to expose a local file server over the network.
variants.hint: Ask which process boundary the connection actually crosses.
variants.explanation: Transport follows the process boundary: stdio for a local subprocess, Streamable HTTP for a remote or shared service.

variants.title: Operate the transport
variants.context: The data layer stays JSON-RPC, but the transport changes connection ownership, authentication, and failure behavior. stdio launches a local subprocess; Streamable HTTP exposes one endpoint over POST and GET with optional server-sent events.
variants.prompt: A shared MCP service must serve many hosts over the network. Which controls belong on that endpoint?
options: Validate Origin, authenticate every request, and support both JSON and event-stream responses.
Accept any Origin and authenticate only the initialize request.
Trust the session ID and skip per-request checks to reduce latency.
optionFeedback: Right: those are the baseline controls for a shared endpoint that anything on the network can reach.
Authenticating only initialization leaves every later request unprotected.
A session ID coordinates protocol state and can never replace authentication.
variants.hint: Ask which process boundary the connection actually crosses.
variants.explanation: A remote endpoint authenticates every request and validates Origin, because reachability is not the same as authorization.

variants.title: Operate the transport
variants.context: The data layer stays JSON-RPC, but the transport changes connection ownership, authentication, and failure behavior. stdio launches a local subprocess; Streamable HTTP exposes one endpoint over POST and GET with optional server-sent events.
variants.prompt: A client finished negotiation with an HTTP server and now sends tool calls. What must each later request carry?
options: The negotiated MCP-Protocol-Version header on every subsequent request.
A repeated initialize request ahead of each tool call.
The session ID alone, since it already names the negotiated session.
optionFeedback: Right: sending the negotiated version on later requests keeps the server from guessing at compatibility.
Initialization happens once per session, and repeating it discards the negotiated state.
A session ID coordinates state but does not tell the server which revision to speak.
variants.hint: Ask what the server would have to guess without it.
variants.explanation: After negotiation, HTTP requests carry the agreed protocol version so both sides stay inside the contract they settled on.
